title: The Monsoon Just Reached Maharashtra on Schedule. Kerala's Late Start Did Not Slow It Down.
excerpt: The southwest monsoon entered Maharashtra on Friday, despite arriving in Kerala three days late. IMD says conditions favour rapid advancement across central India this week.
body:
The southwest monsoon has reached Maharashtra on schedule, covering the Konkan coast, Goa, and parts of the Western Ghats by Friday — making up for a three-day delay in its onset over Kerala and arriving in the state within its normal window. For a country that spent the past week watching anxiously, the news is an early reprieve.

The India Meteorological Department confirmed that the monsoon entered Kerala on June 4, three days after its normal onset date of June 1 and well behind the IMD's earlier forecast of May 26. But once it made landfall, the system advanced rapidly. By June 5, it had covered the entire west coast up to Goa. By Friday, it was in Maharashtra.

"The southwest monsoon has progressed into additional parts of the west-central and east-central Arabian Sea, Karnataka, the entire Goa region, sections of Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh, most parts of Tamil Nadu, and the southwest Bay of Bengal," the IMD said in its latest bulletin.

Why the Speed Matters

The monsoon's rapid advancement after a delayed onset is significant for two reasons. First, it suggests that the atmospheric conditions driving the monsoon — low-level westerly winds, moisture convergence over the Arabian Sea — are stronger than the late Kerala onset implied. Second, it buys time for kharif sowing, which depends on early monsoon rains across Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, and Telangana.

India's agricultural sector, which employs roughly 60 percent of the workforce and contributes 17 to 20 percent of GDP, is acutely sensitive to the monsoon's timing. A delayed or weak monsoon can push up food prices, dampen rural demand, and undercut the government's inflation management — all of which feed into RBI policy and the broader macroeconomic picture.

This year, the stakes are higher than usual. The RBI held its repo rate at 5.25 percent on Friday, with Governor Malhotra citing rising oil prices and monsoon uncertainty among the key external risks. Multiple brokerages have warned of stagflation if oil stays above $95 a barrel and the monsoon disappoints. The monsoon's on-time arrival in Maharashtra takes one of those risks partly off the table.

What the Forecasts Show

The IMD expects the monsoon to advance further into central India, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, and the northeastern states over the next two to three days. By June 10, it could cover large parts of the Western Ghats and begin pushing into Marathwada, where rainfall has been forecast to be above normal.

Pre-monsoon weather activity is already intense. The IMD issued thunderstorm and lightning warnings for Madhya Pradesh on Saturday, with wind speeds gusting up to 70 kilometres per hour in some districts. Mumbai, Konkan, and several interior Maharashtra districts may see rain accompanied by gusty winds until June 8.

The Northern Limit of the Monsoon currently passes through Devgad in Maharashtra's Konkan region, Koppal in Karnataka, Anantapuramu in Andhra Pradesh, and Chennai in Tamil Nadu. These are the advancing edge of a system that will determine the trajectory of India's agricultural season, its inflation outlook, and, ultimately, the economic conditions that shape life for hundreds of millions.

The Diaspora Connection

For NRI families planning summer visits to India, the monsoon's arrival is more than a weather forecast. Travel to the western coast — Mumbai, Goa, Kerala — will be affected by heavy rains and possible flight disruptions over the coming weeks. Those with agricultural land or family connections in rural Maharashtra and Karnataka should expect the monsoon to reach their regions by mid-June.

The monsoon also influences remittance patterns. A good monsoon lifts rural incomes and reduces the financial pressure on families that depend on money sent from abroad. A bad one does the opposite. This year's early signals — a late start but a strong recovery — suggest the season may yet deliver. But the monsoon is not something you can extrapolate from a week's data. The next six weeks will be decisive.

For now, the rain is here, and it is on time.
